content: Can you describe the main situations in your organization that make an expanded WARC Tools suite necessary, and what you need it to help people do in day-to-day archival work?

We’re dealing with much larger web-archive collections now, and the current tools are too limited when staff need to move old ARC holdings into WARC, especially in batches. We also have collections coming from different institutions and different workflows, so people need something that can repack, inspect, deduplicate, and verify content without having to stitch together several separate utilities.
In day-to-day work, archivists need to be able to run these jobs reliably, check what changed after conversion, browse records when something looks odd, and produce reports they can share with colleagues. We also need it to support collaborative testing and deployment, because different institutions are going to use it in slightly different ways but still need consistent results.

Can you walk me through how the current ARC-to-WARC migration process works in your organization today, from start to finish, and where you see the main points of friction, delay, or risk in that workflow?

Right now, someone usually identifies a batch of ARC files, stages them for processing, and then runs the conversion with separate tools or scripts, with a lot of manual checking in between. After that, staff have to inspect the output, compare counts or metadata, and sometimes rerun pieces if something looks off, so it’s not really a smooth end-to-end workflow.
The biggest friction is that the steps aren’t well unified, so people spend time moving between tools and interpreting outputs by hand. The main risks are missed conversion issues, incomplete verification, and difficulty handling large batches consistently, especially when different staff members are doing the work or when we’re collaborating with another institution.
When your team talks about archived web content, what shared terms or definitions do you rely on so that staff at different institutions mean the same thing when they discuss the work?

We rely on the standard format terms pretty heavily, like ARC and WARC, plus things like record, capture, payload, metadata, and duplicate, because those are the common words people use across institutions. In practice, we also need a shared understanding of what counts as a successful migration, a valid record, or a reportable error, since those can vary a bit in everyday conversation.
If anything is ambiguous, we usually have to clarify it in the project group rather than assume everyone means the same thing, so having the tools present consistent terminology would help a lot.

As you think about moving from the current tools into the expanded suite, what does a successful transition look like in your day-to-day archival work, and which parts of the process need the new tools to cover most reliably?

A successful transition would mean staff can keep doing the same core jobs without having to jump between ad hoc scripts and manual checks, and that the results are trustworthy enough to use in production workflows. Ideally, someone can configure a job, run the migration or repackaging, verify the output, and generate a useful report without having to troubleshoot every batch by hand.
The parts that need to be most reliable are the actual ARC-to-WARC conversion, validation of the converted files, duplicate detection, and the reporting that tells us what happened. If those pieces are solid, then the rest of the workflow becomes much easier for archivists and engineers to adopt.

What should the expanded suite do when its results are close enough to look valid but not trustworthy enough for production use, such as whether it should flag them, block downstream use, or route them for manual review?

It should definitely flag them clearly, and for anything that fails the core validation checks I think it should block downstream use until someone reviews it. If a result is only borderline or has warnings rather than hard failures, routing it to manual review makes sense so staff can decide whether it’s acceptable for that collection.
We’d want the distinction between warning and failure to be very clear in the reports, because people need to know quickly whether they can proceed or need to stop and investigate.

When institutional teams need accessibility or learning support for this work, what kinds of help do they usually need most, and what would the expanded suite need to do to fit smoothly into that day-to-day learning and support process?

Usually the biggest need is just clear guidance on what the tools are doing and why a job failed or produced a warning, so people can learn the workflow without having to be experts in the file formats. We also need help that’s easy to use in the moment, like understandable messages, examples of common fixes, and enough context in reports that someone can explain the result to a colleague.
For day-to-day support, the suite should fit into how teams already work, so it shouldn’t require a lot of specialized training just to run routine tasks. If the outputs are readable and the terminology is consistent, that makes it much easier for both new staff and people supporting accessibility needs to use it confidently.

Beyond ARC-to-WARC conversion, repackaging, inspection, reporting, duplicate detection, and post-conversion verification, what other archiving workflow should the expanded WARC Tools suite support for your institution first?

The next thing I’d prioritize is preservation-oriented validation and fix-up before or during conversion, so we can catch obvious problems in the source files earlier. That would include checking file integrity, identifying malformed records, and giving staff a way to triage problem batches instead of discovering issues only after the migration is done.
It would also be helpful if the suite could support batch organization and bookkeeping around the jobs, because that’s a big part of managing large collections. That said, if we had to pick one area to add first, I’d say source validation and triage is the most important.

When you say the suite should support batch organization and bookkeeping, what concrete information should it track for each job and batch, and what should happen when batches are split, merged, rerun, or partially completed?

It should track the basic identifiers for the batch, who submitted it, when it ran, what source collection it came from, and which tools or settings were used. We’d also want status, counts for files and records processed, error and warning totals, and links to any reports or logs so someone can trace what happened later.
If a batch gets split or merged, the relationship to the original job needs to stay visible so we don’t lose the audit trail. For reruns or partial completion, I’d expect the suite to mark exactly what succeeded, what failed, and what was retried, rather than replacing the earlier history, because that kind of transparency matters a lot for preservation work.
For the ARC-to-WARC conversion work, are there any source formats or conversion targets beyond ARC to WARC that the suite needs to support?

ARC to WARC is still the main priority, but we do have some surrounding needs that may come into play, like handling WARC variants or output profiles that different institutions expect for their repositories. I’m not aware of a firm requirement right now for completely different source formats as part of this phase, but there could be legacy edge cases in local collections that we’d want to examine.
So at the moment I’d treat ARC to WARC as the core conversion target, with enough flexibility to accommodate institution-specific packaging or validation rules around the output.

When source files are being validated before or during ARC-to-WARC conversion, what kinds of problems should trigger staff triage versus automatic fix-up, and are there any cases where conversion should proceed despite validation errors?

Automatic fix-up should be limited to small, well-understood issues like minor formatting irregularities that don’t change the meaning of the record, or missing bits that can be safely normalized. Anything that suggests corruption, truncated content, broken headers, or ambiguous metadata should go to staff triage, because we’d rather have a person decide than silently change something important.
Conversion can proceed with some validation errors if they’re non-fatal and clearly documented, but only when the tool can preserve enough context for later review. If there’s any risk that the output would be misleading or not trustworthy, I’d expect the process to stop or at least require explicit confirmation before continuing.

When your tools handle WARC and ARC record data, what is the typical business purpose for inspecting or using that content, and what kinds of record variations or conditions matter most in deciding whether the tool can continue automatically or needs a person to review it?

The main purpose is usually quality control and preservation checking, so staff can confirm the archive is complete, readable, and suitable for long-term access or migration. We also use the record content to diagnose problems, explain anomalies in reports, and verify that the conversion didn’t change anything unexpectedly.
What matters most is whether the record is complete and internally consistent, and whether the headers, payload, and metadata agree with each other. If there are redirects, embedded resources, duplicate captures, or slightly unusual formatting, the tool can often keep going, but if the record looks truncated, corrupt, or contradictory in a way that affects trust, that should trigger human review.

For reporting and verification, which metadata fields must the tools capture or display for each WARC or ARC record, and are there any fields that become mandatory only in certain cases such as incomplete, redirected, or duplicated captures?

At minimum we need the record identifier, capture date and time, source file or batch, record type, target URI or URL, and the basic size or checksum information if it’s available. For verification, it’s also important to show any conversion status, warnings, and the relationship between the source record and the output record so staff can trace lineage.
Some fields become especially important in certain cases, like redirect location, duplicate match information, or an incomplete-record flag. I don’t think we have a hard rule yet that any one of those is universally mandatory in every case, but if the record is incomplete or duplicated, those details need to be visible so the user understands why the tool made a particular decision.

When different institutions collaborate on testing or deployment, what practical rules or handoff conditions should the tool support so each team can work in its own workflow but still get the same conversion, inspection, and verification results?

We’d want the tool to support shared presets or profiles for the core conversion and verification rules, so each institution can run the same logic even if their local workflow is different. It should also preserve the full job history, tool version, and configuration used, because that’s what lets another team reproduce or compare results later.
For handoff, the main condition is that the receiving team can see exactly what was done, what remains unprocessed, and what assumptions were applied. If there are local overrides, those need to be explicit and not hidden, otherwise we lose confidence that both teams are actually testing the same thing.
What minimum level of conversion completeness is acceptable before a batch can be considered successful, and what should the tool do when the output falls short of that level?

A batch should only count as successful if the required conversion and verification steps are complete for everything that was in scope, not just most of it. If there are exceptions, they need to be small, understood, and explicitly accepted by the workflow rather than quietly ignored.
When the output falls short, the tool should mark the batch as partially successful or failed, depending on how serious the gap is, and keep the detailed error information attached. It should not promote the batch to a clean success state unless the missing pieces are clearly accounted for and someone has made a conscious decision to accept them.

As web-archive collections get much larger, what operational rules or limits should the tool follow for splitting, prioritizing, or resuming batch jobs so large-scale ARC-to-WARC processing stays manageable in day-to-day use?

We’d want batch jobs to be split into manageable chunks based on practical collection boundaries, file size, or some other administrator-defined threshold, so one bad item doesn’t block everything else. Priority should probably be configurable, with the ability to resume from the last completed point after an interruption rather than starting over.
In day-to-day use, the key rule is that large jobs need to be restartable, traceable, and not overly dependent on a single long-running process. If a batch is paused or fails partway through, the tool should make it obvious what was completed, what is pending, and what needs human attention before it can continue.

For the web-archive collection growth you mentioned, do you want to specify what “much larger” means in practical terms for deployment planning, or should we leave that scale increase as a tentative assumption for now?

We should leave it as a tentative assumption for now. I can say the tools need to handle noticeably larger batches than a small test set, but I don’t want to lock us into a specific volume until we’ve checked with the institutions about their real collection sizes and infrastructure.

When a large batch is interrupted or paused, what should the tool record and expose so someone can tell exactly which items are complete, which are still pending, and what state is needed to resume it safely?

It should record the job identifier, the exact configuration used, the last completed item or checkpoint, and a per-item status so we can tell completed, pending, failed, or skipped records apart. It also needs to expose any dependencies or prerequisites for resuming, like whether temporary files, intermediate outputs, or validation steps are still intact.
On the display side, the user should be able to see a clear progress summary and a detailed log of where the job stopped. If resuming would risk double-processing or inconsistent output, the tool should flag that before it restarts.

What specific conditions should trigger a safe-resume warning or block before the job restarts—for example, how should the tool judge whether a partially completed run has already produced output that could be duplicated or made inconsistent if resumed?

A warning or block should happen if the tool can’t reliably confirm that the last checkpoint is still valid, or if the output directory already contains records that match the same source items without a clear completion marker. It should also stop and ask for review if the configuration, tool version, or source set has changed since the earlier run, because that can make the resumed results inconsistent.
If there’s any sign that a partially completed run wrote duplicate output, truncated files, or mixed results from different settings, the tool should not resume automatically. In those cases it should force a human to inspect the state and either clean it up or explicitly approve the restart.

When someone is using the expanded suite in the middle of a task, what kinds of guidance, examples, or report context should the tools provide so they can understand what happened and explain it accurately to a colleague without needing specialist knowledge?

The tools should give plain-language summaries alongside the technical details, so someone can quickly see what was processed, what changed, and whether anything needs attention. Examples of the kind of context that helps are record counts, duplicate findings, validation results, and a short explanation of any errors or warnings in terms that archivists can understand.
It would also help if reports clearly show the source collection, the run configuration, and the reason for any skipped or failed items. That way a colleague can hand the report to someone else and they can understand the outcome without having to dig through logs or know the internal processing steps.

When an institution uses a shared preset or profile, what parts of the core conversion and verification rules should be common to everyone, and what kinds of local overrides should be allowed without making the results incompatible with other teams’ runs?

The core conversion and verification rules should be shared, especially anything that affects how ARC is turned into WARC, how integrity is checked, and how duplicates or metadata validation are reported. Those need to stay consistent so different institutions can compare results and trust that the same rules were applied.
Local overrides should be limited to things like paths, storage locations, performance settings, batch size, and maybe institution-specific reporting labels. I’d be cautious about allowing overrides that change the actual conversion logic or validation criteria, because that would make runs harder to compare and could undermine collaboration.

For batch ARC-to-WARC migration, what operational rules should govern how the tool divides work into batches—for example, whether batches are based on source collection boundaries, file counts, size limits, or retry behavior when a batch fails partway through?

The safest rule is to keep batches aligned with source collection boundaries whenever possible, because that makes tracking and reporting much clearer. When collections are too large, the tool should allow subdivision by file count or size limit, but it should do that in a deterministic way so the same inputs produce the same batch layout.
If a batch fails partway through, it should retry only the failed portion if the tool can prove the completed items are intact and won’t be duplicated. If it can’t prove that, it should stop and require a manual decision rather than risking inconsistent output.

When WARC variants are handled as part of packaging and conversion, what specific differences in WARC version, profile, or record structure should the tool recognize and preserve, and are there any variants it should accept only with warnings or reject as incompatible?

It should recognize at least the WARC version, any declared profile, and the record structure differences that affect headers, payload handling, and metadata fields. The key requirement is to preserve whatever variant information is already present so we don’t silently normalize away details that matter for downstream use or comparison.
I’d expect it to accept common, supported variants with normal processing, but warn when the variant is unusual or only partially supported. If a variant would change the meaning of the records or prevents reliable validation and browsing, then it should be rejected as incompatible rather than trying to force it through.

Are there any institution-specific packaging rules for repackaging, such as required output profiles, naming or directory conventions, retention of source identifiers or metadata, or validation steps that need to be applied before the package is considered acceptable?

Yes, there can be institution-specific packaging rules, but they should be expressed as configuration rather than hardcoded behavior. The main things I’d expect are output profile requirements, naming and directory conventions, and rules about carrying forward source identifiers, collection identifiers, and any required metadata into the new package.
Before a package is marked acceptable, it should run the validation steps that the institution requires, such as completeness checks, metadata checks, and any fixity or duplicate checks they rely on. If a local rule conflicts with the shared conversion or verification model, that should be surfaced clearly so the team knows they’re changing the package policy, not just the display.

When staff browse or report on a record, are there any additional metadata fields that become mandatory or especially important only in certain cases—such as redirects, duplicates, or incomplete records—and, if so, what should the tool show in those cases to make the record’s status and lineage clear?

Yes, in those cases a few fields become much more important, especially the source identifier, capture date, original URL, and any relationship fields that show whether the record is a redirect, duplicate, or derived from another record. For incomplete records, I’d also expect the tool to surface what’s missing and whether that affects preservation or just display.
The tool should make the status very explicit in the browse and report views, with a clear label and a short explanation of why the record is marked that way. It should also show lineage or provenance details so staff can tell where the record came from and whether it points to or depends on another record.

When the tool connects to a repository or storage system, are there any required behaviors for reading from, writing to, or syncing with that system—such as where it should store outputs, how it should handle access or connection failures, or whether it needs to preserve links back to the source repository?

Yes, it should be very explicit about where outputs are written and what source system they belong to, so we can trace a package back to the repository or storage location it came from. Preserving links or reference information back to the source repository is important, especially for audit and later verification.
For failures, the tool should fail cleanly, log the reason in plain terms, and not leave half-written outputs looking complete. If access or connection is interrupted, it should pause or stop in a way that lets staff recover without guessing what was already committed and what still needs to be rerun.

When access or connection is interrupted during a transfer or write, what should the tool do to make the failure and recovery state clear—for example, should it record what was completed, what was not, and any steps staff need to rerun?

Yes, it should record exactly what was completed, what was left incomplete, and the point where the failure happened. That way staff can tell whether they need to rerun the whole job or just the failed part.
It should also write a recovery status that is easy to read in logs and reports, including any rerun steps or cleanup needed before retrying. The main thing is that nobody should have to infer the state from partial files alone.

For collaborative handoff during ARC to WARC conversion, are there any specific conditions under which the receiving team should see different levels of detail about what was completed, what remains unprocessed, and any local assumptions or overrides—for example, for partial runs, reruns, or mixed-source jobs?

Yes, different detail levels make sense depending on the handoff scenario. For a normal completed run, the receiving team probably only needs a concise summary, but for partial runs, reruns, or mixed-source jobs they need much more detail about what was processed, what was skipped, and any overrides or local assumptions that affected the result.
In those cases, the tool should surface the exact job state, the boundaries of each processed segment, and any warnings about data that may not compare cleanly across sources. The goal is that the receiving team can take over without having to reconstruct the workflow from logs.

For shared jobs, what specific information should the audit trail retain beyond the job history, tool version, and configuration—such as local overrides, access context, or comparison notes—so another team can reproduce the run or understand why their results might differ?

It should retain any local overrides, the access or permissions context used at the time, and any comparison or reconciliation notes that explain why the run behaved the way it did. If staff applied a manual decision, skipped a validation, or accepted a warning, that should be captured too.
For reproducibility, I’d also want the trail to include the exact input set, the source and target locations, and any environment details that could affect parsing or packaging. That way another team can tell whether they’re seeing a real difference in the data or just a difference in setup.

When maintenance or updates are needed, how should ownership be handled across institutions so it’s clear who is responsible for fixes, coordination, and communication when multiple teams use the same tools?

Ownership should be explicit at both the local and shared levels. Each institution should know who is responsible for its own configuration, data, and operational issues, while the shared tool maintainers handle the common codebase, release coordination, and broader defect fixes.
For communication, there should be a clear escalation path so teams know whether to contact their local admin, the shared support group, or the development team. The main thing is avoiding ambiguity when several institutions are using the same workflow but only one of them is seeing the problem.

When a problem affects only one institution in a shared workflow, what concrete rules should determine whether it is handled by the local admin, the shared support group, or the development team, especially if the issue could be either a site-specific configuration problem or a broader product defect?

If it can be tied to that institution’s configuration, permissions, source data, or environment, it should start with the local admin. If the same behavior shows up at more than one institution or can be reproduced with a standard setup, then it should move to the shared support group and likely the development team.
If it’s ambiguous, I’d want the tool or process to capture enough evidence to classify it quickly, like logs, settings, and the exact job parameters. The key rule is to avoid bouncing the issue around without first checking whether it reproduces outside the local environment.

What specific evidence should the process capture at the first point of triage so the team can decide quickly whether the issue reproduces outside the local environment and should stay with the local admin or escalate to shared support?

It should capture the exact job parameters, the source and target identifiers, the tool version, and the relevant configuration in effect at the time. I’d also want the key logs, the error message or failure point, and any local overrides or access context that might have changed behavior.
If possible, it should include a small reproducible sample or a pointer to the affected record set so someone else can try it in a controlled setup. That usually gives enough evidence to tell whether it’s a local issue or something the shared team needs to investigate.
Are there any features in the expanded tool suite that you’d explicitly be comfortable deferring to a later release, and what makes them lower priority or dependent on other work?

Yes, I’d be comfortable deferring some of the more convenience-oriented features, like richer browsing views or polished comparison dashboards, if that helps us get the core migration, validation, and reporting functions out first. Those are useful, but they don’t block the main archival workflow in the same way.
I’d also treat any very specialized institution-specific customizations as later work unless they’re needed by several sites, because they tend to depend on local policies and extra testing. Anything that relies on a stable core audit, conversion, and error-handling layer probably has to wait until that foundation is solid.

When outputs are repackaged into a new package or bundle, what specific rules should determine how the source repository reference is carried forward—such as whether each package, record, or file needs its own trace link, and what should happen if the original source location is unavailable or has changed?

Each output package should keep a top-level trace link back to the original source repository, and I’d expect individual records or files to carry their own trace references if the conversion splits or rearranges content in a way that would otherwise make provenance unclear. If the package is simple and one-to-one, the package-level link may be enough, but once things are aggregated or transformed, you really want finer-grained traceability.
If the original source location is unavailable or has moved, the tool should preserve whatever stable identifier or archived reference was available at conversion time and mark the live location as unresolved rather than inventing a replacement. That way the lineage stays honest even if the original endpoint can’t be reached later.
What legacy ARC-to-WARC edge cases should we plan for in local collections, such as unusual record structures, embedded content, or malformed source files, and how should the tool handle them?

We should plan for odd record layouts, embedded or nested content, and malformed ARC files that don’t quite follow the expected structure. In practice that means some records may need to be passed through with warnings, while others may have to fail cleanly if the tool can’t preserve integrity.
The important part is that the tool should be explicit about what it could convert, what it had to skip, and what it repaired or normalized. Archivists need to know when the output is faithful and when there was a compromise so they can decide whether a collection needs manual review.

When the tool compares a converted WARC against the source or an expected reference, what kinds of local preset overrides, if any, should be allowed to affect duplicate detection or verification behavior without changing the underlying validation rules?

Local presets should be allowed to adjust the comparison thresholds and presentation, not the actual validation logic. For example, a site might choose to ignore certain known harmless differences, change how aggressively near-duplicates are flagged, or set a local allowlist for expected metadata variations.
What I would not want is a preset that silently changes what counts as valid content or metadata. The core verification rules should stay consistent, and the local override should only control how results are grouped, filtered, or reported for that institution.

For the convenience-oriented features you’re deferring, are there any deployment or institutional conditions where a site would still need limited versions of browsing or dashboard capabilities at launch—for example to support local training, oversight, or communication with stakeholders?

Yes, in some institutions we’d still need a very minimal browsing view at launch, mainly so staff can confirm that a migration landed correctly and do basic training or spot checks. I’d also expect a simple status or summary dashboard if local managers need to report progress to stakeholders or track batch health during rollout.
What I’d keep limited is depth and polish, not the presence of those functions altogether. If we can show a small, reliable set of records, job outcomes, and warnings, that’s usually enough for early deployment.

For that minimal launch browsing view, what should staff be able to do with it in practice—such as which record details must be visible, what warnings or statuses must appear, and what should be hidden or blocked until later?

Staff should be able to see the basic record identity, source and target links, timestamps, MIME type, and whether the record passed conversion and verification. Any warnings, skipped fields, checksum or metadata mismatches, and provenance notes should be visible right there so they can judge whether the item needs review.
What should stay blocked is anything that lets them edit the preserved content or change the validation result from the browsing view. I’d also hide any advanced analysis or bulk-management functions until later, because the launch version should support inspection and confidence-building, not curation from the browser.

When staff are browsing records, are there any limited actions they should still be allowed to take from that view, such as adding review notes, creating a follow-up task, or opening a separate correction workflow, as long as they cannot alter the preserved content or the validation result itself?

Yes, I’d be comfortable with lightweight actions like adding a review note, flagging a record for follow-up, or opening a correction workflow in a separate system. Those are helpful for operations and training, and they don’t interfere with the preserved content or the official validation outcome.
I’d keep those actions clearly separated from the record itself, though, so it’s obvious that the archive data is read-only. If someone needs to correct something, that should happen through a controlled workflow with its own audit trail.

When a batch has to be split by file count or size limit, are there any operational boundaries you want to define—for example how to keep the split reproducible, and what specific proof is needed before allowing a partial retry instead of sending the job to manual review?

Yes, the split should be reproducible from the original batch definition so we can rerun the same boundaries if needed. I’d expect the tool to record exactly how the cut was made, including the file count or size threshold and the ordering rule used, so a later retry doesn’t reshuffle things.
For a partial retry, I’d want proof that the failed segment is isolated and that the successful pieces are already verified and immutable. If there’s any ambiguity about whether the split changed the package content or the failure might have affected upstream records, then it should go to manual review instead of retrying automatically.
